text: A 3-credit course taught by Prof. Hugo de Souza Oliveira. These are the lecture notes for the course.

title: Fundamentals of Mechanical Vibrations
text:
Course Notes


Class 2 — Springs, Dampers & Free Vibration
Combining springs and dampers in series and parallel. Deriving the equation of motion from a free body diagram. Natural frequency. Free vibration response and initial conditions.
Interactive: Free vibration explorer — change \(m\), \(k\), \(u_0\), \(v_0\).


Class 3 — Forced Vibration (Undamped)
Harmonic excitation of an undamped system. Homogeneous and particular solutions. Resonance. Phase shift and the phasor diagram. Introduction to damped forced vibration.
Interactive: Frequency response and time-domain explorer.


Class 4 — Damped Forced Vibration & Dimensionless Form
Completing the damped forced response derivation. Amplitude \(U\) and phase \(\phi\). Behaviour at resonance. Dimensionless parameters (\(\zeta\), \(r\), \(c_c\)). Bode plots.
Interactive: Bode plot explorer — drag \(\zeta\) and overlay multiple curves.


Class 5 — Free Damped Systems
Euler identity and complex notation. Characteristic equation. Underdamped, critically damped, and overdamped cases. Logarithmic decrement for experimental damping identification.
Interactive: Free response explorer — watch the transition between all three regimes.


Class 6 — Transmissibility
Force transmissibility and motion transmissibility. The isolation threshold at \(r = \sqrt{2}\). Base excitation: relative and absolute displacement. The damping trade-off.
Interactive: Transmissibility explorer — drag \(\zeta\) and \(r\), overlay \(U/Y\) and \(T_F\), compare curves.


Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
From SDOF to two-degree-of-freedom systems. Coupled equations of motion. Matrix form. Eigenvalue problem. Natural frequencies and mode shapes for the general and symmetric cases.
Interactive: Natural frequencies and mode shapes explorer — change \(m_1\), \(m_2\), \(k_1\), \(k_2\).


Class 8 — Forced Vibration & Dynamic Vibration Absorber
Forced 2DOF response. Dynamic stiffness matrix. Resonance and anti-resonance. The dynamic vibration absorber: tuning condition, physical interpretation, and design.
Interactive: DVA frequency response explorer — change mass ratio \(\mu\) and tuning ratio \(f\).

title: Class 5 — Free Damped Systems
text:
Before analysing the free damped response, we introduce a powerful mathematical tool: complex exponential notation, based on Euler’s identity. This will significantly simplify our calculations going forward.


From Euler, we know:
\[e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\]
For a time-varying angle \(\theta = \omega t\), this becomes:
\[e^{i\omega t} = \cos(\omega t) + i\sin(\omega t)\]
Therefore, a sinusoidal motion can be represented as either the real or imaginary part of a complex exponential:
\[\cos(\omega t) = \text{Re}\!\left(e^{i\omega t}\right), \qquad \sin(\omega t) = \text{Im}\!\left(e^{i\omega t}\right)\]



The real advantage appears when differentiating. If \(u(t) = Ue^{i\omega t}\), then:
\[\dot{u}(t) = i\omega\, U e^{i\omega t}, \qquad \ddot{u}(t) = -\omega^2\, U e^{i\omega t}\]
Differentiation becomes multiplication — an enormous simplification.



Replacing the excitation \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\) with \(F_0 e^{i\omega t}\) (we take the imaginary part of the solution at the end):
\[m\ddot{u} + c\dot{u} + ku = F_0 e^{i\omega t}\]
With \(u(t) = Ue^{i\omega t}\):
\[m(-\omega^2)Ue^{i\omega t} + c(i\omega)Ue^{i\omega t} + kUe^{i\omega t} = F_0 e^{i\omega t}\]
Dividing through by \(e^{i\omega t}\):
\[U\bigl(k - m\omega^2 + ic\omega\bigr) = F_0\]
\[U = \frac{F_0}{k - m\omega^2 + ic\omega}\]
To extract the amplitude, multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate \((a - ib)\), where \(a = k - m\omega^2\) and \(b = c\omega\):
\[U = \frac{F_0}{a + ib}\cdot\frac{a - ib}{a - ib} = \frac{F_0(a-ib)}{a^2+b^2}\]
\[U = \frac{F_0\,a}{a^2+b^2} - i\,\frac{F_0\,b}{a^2+b^2}\]
Then we compute the modulus:
\[|U| = \sqrt{\left(\frac{F_0 a}{a^2+b^2}\right)^{\!2} + \left(\frac{F_0 b}{a^2+b^2}\right)^{\!2}} = \frac{F_0\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}{a^2+b^2} = \frac{F_0}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\]
\[\boxed{|U| = \frac{F_0}{\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}}\]
This is exactly the same result from Class 4 — now obtained in a few lines. Complex notation is the standard tool in vibration analysis.

title: Class 5 — Free Damped Systems
section: 5.2 Free Vibration of a Damped System
text:
5.2 Free Vibration of a Damped System
We now turn to the free (unforced) response of the damped 1-DOF system. Using the dimensionless equation from Class 4 (with right-hand side equal to zero):
\[\ddot{u} + 2\zeta\omega_n\dot{u} + \omega_n^2 u = 0\]

General Trial Solution
To find the solution in all cases simultaneously, we propose the general trial solution:
\[u(t) = Ce^{st}\]
where \(s\) is a complex number to be determined. This is the most general trial function — depending on whether \(s\) is real or complex, it will represent exponential decay, oscillation, or both.
Substituting:
\[s^2 Ce^{st} + 2\zeta\omega_n s\, Ce^{st} + \omega_n^2 Ce^{st} = 0\]
Dividing by \(Ce^{st} \neq 0\):






ImportantCharacteristic Equation



\[\boxed{s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2 = 0}\]
The two roots of this equation completely determine the nature of the free response.


Applying the quadratic formula:
\[s = -\zeta\omega_n \pm \omega_n\sqrt{\zeta^2 - 1}\]
The term \(\sqrt{\zeta^2 - 1}\) changes character depending on \(\zeta\):

If \(0 < \zeta < 1\): \(\zeta^2 - 1 < 0\) → complex roots → oscillatory decay
If \(\zeta = 1\): \(\zeta^2 - 1 = 0\) → repeated real root → fastest non-oscillatory decay
If \(\zeta > 1\): \(\zeta^2 - 1 > 0\) → two distinct real roots → pure exponential decay

title: Class 5 — Free Damped Systems
text:
Case 1 — Underdamped System (\(0 < \zeta < 1\))
Since \(\zeta^2 - 1 < 0\), we write \(\sqrt{\zeta^2 - 1} = i\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\). Defining the damped natural frequency:
\[\omega_d = \omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\]
the two complex conjugate roots are:
\[s_{1,2} = -\zeta\omega_n \pm i\omega_d\]
The general solution is therefore:
\[u(t) = e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}\bigl[A\cos(\omega_d t) + B\sin(\omega_d t)\bigr]\]
or equivalently (introducing amplitude \(V\) and phase \(\psi\)):






ImportantUnderdamped Free Response



\[\boxed{u(t) = V\,e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}\,\cos(\omega_d t - \psi)}\]

The exponential envelope \(Ve^{-\zeta\omega_n t}\) causes the amplitude to decay toward zero.
The oscillatory part \(\cos(\omega_d t - \psi)\) produces a sinusoidal waveform at frequency \(\omega_d < \omega_n\).
Both \(V\) and \(\psi\) are determined by initial conditions.



Note that \(\omega_d < \omega_n\) because \(\sqrt{1-\zeta^2} < 1\). Damping lowers the oscillation frequency in addition to reducing the amplitude.


            u t         u₁    u₂   T_d  e^(−ζω_n t)


Underdamped free response: oscillation at \(\omega_d\) contained within an exponentially decaying envelope \(e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}\). Peaks \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) are separated by one damped period \(T_d\).

title: Class 5 — Free Damped Systems
text:
5.3 Logarithmic Decrement
A key application of underdamped free vibration is experimental damping identification. Given measured free vibration data, we can extract \(\zeta\) from the ratio of successive peaks. The interactive below shows which peaks are being compared and computes \(\delta\) and \(\zeta\) live.


Code
viewof zeta_ld = Inputs.range([0.02, 0.5], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "Damping ratio  ζ"})
viewof wn_ld   = Inputs.range([0.5, 10],  {value: 2.0, step: 0.5,  label: "Natural frequency  ωₙ  (rad/s)"})
viewof peak_n  = Inputs.range([1, 5],     {value: 1,   step: 1,    label: "Compare peak n  with peak n+1"})

























Code
wd_ld  = wn_ld * Math.sqrt(1 - zeta_ld**2)
Td_ld  = 2 * Math.PI / wd_ld
tEnd_ld = (peak_n + 2.5) * Td_ld
dt_ld  = tEnd_ld / 600

function u_ld(t) {
  return Math.exp(-zeta_ld * wn_ld * t) * Math.cos(wd_ld * t)
}

data_ld = Array.from({length: 601}, (_, i) => ({t: i * dt_ld, u: u_ld(i * dt_ld)}))

// Peak times: cosine peaks at t = n * Td
t1_ld = (peak_n - 1) * Td_ld
t2_ld = peak_n * Td_ld
u1_ld = u_ld(t1_ld)
u2_ld = u_ld(t2_ld)
delta_ld = Math.log(u1_ld / u2_ld)
zeta_from_delta = delta_ld / Math.sqrt(4 * Math.PI**2 + delta_ld**2)
























































































Code
Plot.plot({
  title: "Log-Decrement: Consecutive Peaks",
  marks: [

Derivation
For two consecutive peaks at times \(t_1\) and \(t_1 + T_d\) (where \(T_d = 2\pi/\omega_d\) is the damped period):
\[u_1 = V\,e^{-\zeta\omega_n t_1}\cos(\omega_d t_1 - \psi)\] \[u_2 = V\,e^{-\zeta\omega_n(t_1+T_d)}\cos(\omega_d(t_1+T_d) - \psi)\]
Since at consecutive peaks the cosine has the same value, the ratio is:
\[\frac{u_1}{u_2} = \frac{e^{-\zeta\omega_n t_1}}{e^{-\zeta\omega_n(t_1+T_d)}} = e^{\zeta\omega_n T_d}\]
Taking the natural logarithm:
\[\delta = \ln\!\left(\frac{u_1}{u_2}\right) = \zeta\omega_n T_d = \zeta\omega_n \cdot \frac{2\pi}{\omega_d} = \frac{2\pi\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\]






ImportantLogarithmic Decrement



\[\boxed{\delta = \ln\!\left(\frac{u_1}{u_2}\right) = \frac{2\pi\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}}\]
Measuring damping in practice: Record the free vibration signal, identify two peaks, and compute:
\[\zeta = \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2 + \delta^2}}\]
For small damping (\(\zeta \ll 1\)), \(\sqrt{1-\zeta^2} \approx 1\) and \(\delta \approx 2\pi\zeta\), so:
\[\zeta \approx \frac{\delta}{2\pi}\]

Class 3 — Forced Vibration of Undamped Systems
text:
From the previous class, the equation of motion for a 1-DOF undamped system is:
\[m\ddot{u}(t) + ku(t) = 0\]
and its general solution is:
\[u(t) = \frac{v_0}{\omega_n\cos\phi}\,\sin\!\left(\omega_n t + \phi\right), \qquad \phi = \arctan\!\left(\frac{u_0\,\omega_n}{v_0}\right), \qquad \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\]
where \(u_0 = u(0)\) is the initial displacement and \(v_0 = \dot{u}(0)\) is the initial velocity. The system oscillates indefinitely at \(\omega_n\), since there is no energy dissipation.

title: Class 3 — Forced Vibration of Undamped Systems
text:
3.1 The Forced Undamped System
A real structure is rarely left to vibrate freely. It is typically driven by some external force. The simplest and most important case is a harmonic excitation:
\[F(t) = F_0 \sin(\omega t)\]
where \(F_0\) is the force amplitude and \(\omega\) is the excitation frequency. The equation of motion becomes:
\[\boxed{m\ddot{u}(t) + ku(t) = F_0\sin(\omega t)}\]






WarningDo not confuse \(\omega\) and \(\omega_n\)



\(\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}\) is the natural frequency — a property of the system. \(\omega\) is the excitation frequency — a property of the loading. We can choose \(\omega\) freely.



Solution Structure
From differential equations theory, the complete solution is the sum of two parts:
\[u(t) = \underbrace{u_h(t)}_{\substack{\text{free / natural}\\\text{response}}} + \underbrace{u_p(t)}_{\substack{\text{forced / particular}\\\text{response}}}\]
From the previous class, the natural response is:
\[u_h(t) = A\sin(\omega_n t + \phi)\]
For the forced response, we propose a particular solution of the form:
\[u_p(t) = U\sin(\omega t)\]
Since there is no damping, both components persist indefinitely: they sum to give the complete behavior of the system.

title: Class 3 — Forced Vibration of Undamped Systems
text:
3.5 Introduction to Damped Systems
Systems without damping are an idealization. Real structures dissipate energy through viscous friction, internal material damping, dry friction (Coulomb), and other mechanisms. Adding damping makes the model physically realistic and, crucially, removes the singularity at resonance.
The forced equation of motion for a damped system is:
\[m\ddot{u} + c\dot{u} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)\]
where the double underline on \(c\dot{u}\) reminds us this is the new term.

Why Does Damping Require a Cosine Term?
In the undamped case, a pure sine \(u_p = U\sin(\omega t)\) worked as a particular solution. With damping, however, the \(c\dot{u}\) term introduces a component proportional to \(\cos(\omega t)\). Therefore, we must try a two-component particular solution:
\[u_p(t) = A\sin(\omega t) + B\cos(\omega t)\]

The cosine term \(B\cos(\omega t)\) represents the 90°-delayed part of the response that only exists because of damping. If \(c = 0\), we will find \(B = 0\) and recover the undamped result.



Setting Up the Algebra
Computing derivatives:
\[\dot{u}_p = A\omega\cos(\omega t) - B\omega\sin(\omega t)\] \[\ddot{u}_p = -A\omega^2\sin(\omega t) - B\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\]
Substituting into the equation of motion and grouping terms by \(\sin(\omega t)\) and \(\cos(\omega t)\):
For \(\sin(\omega t)\):
\[A(k - m\omega^2) - cB\omega = F_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \alpha = F_0\]
For \(\cos(\omega t)\):
\[B(k - m\omega^2) + cA\omega = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \beta = 0\]
Let us define \(D = k - m\omega^2\) for convenience. Then:
\[\begin{cases} AD - cB\omega = F_0 \\ BD + cA\omega = 0 \end{cases}\]
Solving this \(2\times 2\) system (details shown in Class 4):
\[A = \frac{F_0(k-m\omega^2)}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}, \qquad B = \frac{-F_0 c\omega}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}\]
The physical amplitude and phase of the response are:
\[U = \sqrt{A^2+B^2} = \frac{F_0}{\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}, \qquad \phi = \arctan\!\left(\frac{c\omega}{k-m\omega^2}\right)\]
The complete derivation and the dimensionless form are covered in Class 4.

title: Class 2 — Springs, Dampers & Equation of Motion
text:
In the previous class we understood the role of springs and dampers as the fundamental passive elements in a vibrating mechanical system. Now we address two important questions:

What is the equivalent stiffness/damping when elements are combined?
Once we know all the elements, how do we obtain the equation of motion that governs the dynamics of the whole system?

title: Class 2 — Springs, Dampers & Equation of Motion
text:
Combining Springs

Single Spring
The constitutive relation of a linear spring is:
\[F = k\, u \quad \Longrightarrow \quad u = \frac{F}{k}\]
where \(k\) is the stiffness (N/m), \(u\) is the elongation (m), and \(F\) is the applied force (N).



Simple Spring




Springs in Parallel
When two springs share the same displacement \(u\), the forces add:
\[F = F_1 + F_2 = k_1 u + k_2 u = (k_1+k_2)\,u\]
So the equivalent stiffness is:
\[\boxed{k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 + k_2}\]



Springs in Parallel


If we have more than two springs, we have then
\[\boxed{k_1 + k_2 + \cdots + k_n}\]
The equivalent stiffness is simply the sum of the individual stiffnesses.



Springs in Series
When two springs are connected end-to-end, the same force \(F\) passes through both and the displacements add:
\[u = u_1 + u_2 = \frac{F}{k_1} + \frac{F}{k_2} = F\!\left(\frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2}\right)\]
So the equivalent stiffness is:
\[\boxed{\frac{1}{k_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2}}\]



Springs in Series


If we have more springs in series, we have then
\[\boxed{\frac{1}{k_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{k_n}}\]
in which \(n\) represents the number of springs.

title: Class 2 — Springs, Dampers & Equation of Motion
text:
Combining Dampers

Single Damper
The constitutive relation of a linear (viscous) damper is:
\[F = c\,\dot{u}\]
where \(c\) is the damping coefficient (N·s/m) and \(\dot{u}\) is the relative velocity.



Simple Viscous Damper




Dampers in Parallel
When two dampers share the same velocity \(\dot{u}\), the forces add — exactly analogous to springs in parallel:
\[F = c_1\dot{u} + c_2\dot{u} = (c_1+c_2)\,\dot{u}\]
\[\boxed{c_{\text{eq}} = c_1 + c_2}\]



Dampers in Parallel


Again, for more dampers the equivalent damping will be
\[c_{eq} = c_1 + c_2 + \cdots + c_n\]


Dampers in Series
When two dampers are connected in series, the same force acts on both and the velocities add:
\[\dot{u} = \dot{u}_1 + \dot{u}_2 = \frac{F_e}{c_1} + \frac{F_e}{c_2}\]
\[\boxed{\frac{1}{c_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{c_1}+\frac{1}{c_2}}\]



Dampers in series


One more time, for more than one damper, we have
\[\frac{1}{c_{eq}} = \frac{1}{c_1} + \frac{1}{c_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{c_n}\]
Here, \(n\) is the number of dampers.

title: Class 2 — Springs, Dampers & Equation of Motion
text:
Equation of Motion
Now that we understand the basic elements that constitute a simple mechanical system,. Let’s understand how to obtain the equation of motion. Consider a mass \(m\) supported by a spring \(k\) and a damper \(c\) in parallel, subjected to displacement \(u\) (positive upward).



Mechanical System 1DOF


The Free Body Diagram (FBD) shows two forces acting on the mass, both opposing the positive \(u\) direction:

Spring force: \(F_s = - ku\) (downward)
Damping force: \(F_e = - c\dot{u}\) (downward)

Applying Newton’s second law (\(\sum F = m\ddot{u}\)) in the positive direction:
\[m\ddot{u} = -ku - c\dot{u}\]
Rearranging:






ImportantEquation of Motion — 1-DOF System



\[\boxed{m\ddot{u} + c\dot{u} + ku = 0}\]



Term
Name




\(m\ddot{u}\)
Inertia force


\(c\dot{u}\)
Damping force


\(ku\)
Elastic (spring) force



Any external excitation adds a right-hand side: \(m\ddot{u} + c\dot{u} + ku = F(t)\) because of the balance of forces.

title: Class 2 — Springs, Dampers & Equation of Motion
text:
Exercises

Exercise 1 — System with Two Spring-Damper Pairs in Parallel
Find the equation of motion of the system below, where two spring-damper pairs \((c_1,k_1)\) and \((c_2,k_2)\) are arranged in parallel between the ground and the mass \(m\).





Solution. The FBD gives four forces acting downward on the mass: \(c_1\dot{u}\), \(k_1 u\), \(c_2\dot{u}\), and \(k_2 u\). Applying Newton’s second law:
\[m\ddot{u} = -c_1\dot{u} - k_1 u - c_2\dot{u} - k_2 u\]
Rearranging:
\[\boxed{m\ddot{u} + \underbrace{(c_1+c_2)}_{c_{\text{eq}}}\dot{u} + \underbrace{(k_1+k_2)}_{k_{\text{eq}}}u = 0}\]

Note: The equivalent stiffness and damping are both sums — confirming the parallel combination rules.




Exercise 2 — The Simple Pendulum
Find the equation of motion of a simple pendulum of length \(l\) and mass \(m\).





Key insight: only one coordinate — the angle \(\theta\) — is needed to describe the entire configuration. This is a 1-DOF system.
For a rotating body, Newton’s second law becomes the moment equation about the pivot \(O\):
\[\sum M_O = J_O\,\ddot\theta\]
The only moment is due to gravity. The tangential component of gravity is \(mg\sin\theta\), acting at distance \(l\):
\[-mgl\sin\theta = J_O\,\ddot\theta\]
The moment of inertia of a point mass about \(O\) is \(J_O = ml^2\), so:
\[ml^2\ddot\theta = -mgl\sin\theta\]
Dividing by \(ml^2\) and applying the small-angle approximation (\(\sin\theta \approx \theta\) for \(\theta \approx 0\)):
\[\boxed{\ddot\theta + \frac{g}{l}\,\theta = 0}\]
This has exactly the same structure as \(m\ddot{u} + ku = 0\), with the identification \(k/m \leftrightarrow g/l\).

title: Class 2 — Springs, Dampers & Equation of Motion
text:
Free Vibration Response
We now solve the undamped free equation of motion:
\[m\ddot{u} + ku = 0\]

Proposed Solution
By intuition, we expect the system to oscillate. We propose:
\[u(t) = A\sin(\omega_n t + \phi)\]
Computing the derivatives:
\[\dot{u}(t) = A\omega_n\cos(\omega_n t + \phi), \qquad \ddot{u}(t) = -A\omega_n^2\sin(\omega_n t+\phi)\]
Substituting into the equation of motion:
\[-m\omega_n^2 A\sin(\omega_n t+\phi) + kA\sin(\omega_n t+\phi) = 0\]
\[A\sin(\omega_n t+\phi)\bigl(k - m\omega_n^2\bigr) = 0\]
This must hold for all \(t\), so:
\[k - m\omega_n^2 = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \omega_n^2 = \frac{k}{m}\]






ImportantNatural Frequency



\[\boxed{\omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}} \quad \text{[rad/s]}\]
The natural frequency tells us how quickly the system exchanges kinetic and potential energy. A stiffer or lighter system vibrates faster.


The period of oscillation and the frequency in Hz are:
\[T_n = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_n}, \qquad f_n = \frac{\omega_n}{2\pi}\]


Determining \(A\) and \(\phi\) from Initial Conditions
The constants \(A\) (amplitude) and \(\phi\) (phase angle) are fixed by the initial conditions \(u(0) = u_0\) and \(\dot{u}(0) = v_0\):
\[u(0) = A\sin(\phi) = u_0\] \[\dot{u}(0) = A\omega_n\cos(\phi) = v_0\]
Dividing:
\[\tan\phi = \frac{u_0\omega_n}{v_0} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \phi = \arctan\!\left(\frac{u_0\,\omega_n}{v_0}\right)\]
And the amplitude:
\[A = \sqrt{u_0^2 + \left(\frac{v_0}{\omega_n}\right)^2}\]
The complete solution is:
\[\boxed{u(t) = \sqrt{u_0^2 + \left(\frac{v_0}{\omega_n}\right)^2}\;\sin\!\left(\omega_n t + \arctan\!\frac{u_0\,\omega_n}{v_0}\right)}\]

title: Class 2 — Springs, Dampers & Equation of Motion
Class 4 — Damped Forced Vibration & Dimensionless Form
text:
Systems without damping are an idealization. Real structures dissipate energy through damping — viscous, dry friction, and other mechanisms.
In undamped systems, the free response \(u_h(t)\) never disappears:
\[u(t) = u_h(t) + u_p(t)\]
Damping introduces energy dissipation to our systems, and they become physically realistic: \(u_h(t)\) eventually decays, leaving only the steady-state particular response \(u_p(t)\).
Our forced damped system is governed by:
\[\boxed{m\ddot{u} + \underset{=}{c\dot{u}} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)}\]
Similarly to the undamped case, we try a particular solution:
\[u_p(t) = A\sin(\omega t) + B\cos(\omega t)\]






WarningWhy a cosine term?



In the undamped case, a pure sine \(u_p = U\sin(\omega t)\) was sufficient. With damping, the \(c\dot{u}\) term introduces a component proportional to \(\cos(\omega t)\), so we need two components. If \(c = 0\), we will find \(B = 0\) and recover the undamped result.




Computing derivatives of the trial solution:
\[\dot{u}_p(t) = A\omega\cos(\omega t) - B\omega\sin(\omega t)\] \[\ddot{u}_p(t) = -A\omega^2\sin(\omega t) - B\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\]
Substituting into the equation of motion term by term:

Inertia term: \(m\ddot{u}_p = -mA\omega^2\sin(\omega t) - mB\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\)
Damping term: \(c\dot{u}_p = \phantom{-}cA\omega\cos(\omega t) - cB\omega\sin(\omega t)\)
Elastic term: \(ku_p = \phantom{-m}kA\sin(\omega t) + kB\cos(\omega t)\)

Grouping by \(\sin(\omega t)\) and \(\cos(\omega t)\) and setting equal to \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\):
\[\underbrace{[A(k-m\omega^2) - cB\omega]}_{\alpha}\sin(\omega t) + \underbrace{[B(k-m\omega^2) + cA\omega]}_{\beta}\cos(\omega t) = F_0\sin(\omega t)\]
For this to hold at all times \(t\):
\[\alpha = F_0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \beta = 0\]
Defining \(D = k - m\omega^2\) for convenience:
\[\begin{cases} AD - cB\omega = F_0 \\ BD + cA\omega = 0 \end{cases}\]
Solving this \(2\times 2\) system:
\[\boxed{A = \frac{F_0 D}{D^2+(c\omega)^2} = \frac{F_0(k-m\omega^2)}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}\]
\[\boxed{B = -\frac{c\omega A}{D} = \frac{-F_0 c\omega}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}\]
Therefore:
\[u_p(t) = A\sin(\omega t) + B\cos(\omega t)\]



The two components play different roles:

\(A\sin(\omega t)\): can only be in phase (\(A > 0\)) or 180° delayed (\(A < 0\)) relative to \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\).
\(B\cos(\omega t)\): is always 90° delayed relative to \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\).

Note that \(B = -F_0 c\omega\big/[D^2 + (c\omega)^2]\): if \(c = 0\) then \(B = 0\) — the 90°-delayed component only exists because of damping \(c\).

title: Class 4 — Damped Forced Vibration & Dimensionless Form
text:
From Class 3 we left with the equation of motion for a damped forced 1-DOF system:
\[m\ddot{u} + c\dot{u} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)\]
and a particular solution ansatz \(u_p(t) = A\sin(\omega t) + B\cos(\omega t)\). This class completes the derivation and introduces the powerful dimensionless form.

title: Class 4 — Damped Forced Vibration & Dimensionless Form
text:
2 4.1 Solving for A and B
Recall from Class 3 that after substituting the ansatz into the equation of motion and grouping trigonometric terms, we obtained (with \(D = k - m\omega^2\)):
\[\begin{cases} AD - cB\omega = F_0 \\ BD + cA\omega = 0 \end{cases}\]
From the second equation: \(B = -\dfrac{cA\omega}{D}\). Substituting into the first:
\[AD - c\omega\!\left(-\frac{cA\omega}{D}\right) = F_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad A\frac{D^2 + c^2\omega^2}{D} = F_0\]
\[\boxed{A = \frac{F_0 D}{D^2+(c\omega)^2} = \frac{F_0(k-m\omega^2)}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}\]
\[\boxed{B = -\frac{c\omega A}{D} = \frac{-F_0 c\omega}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}\]

2.1 Physical Interpretation of A and B
The response \(u_p(t) = A\sin(\omega t) + B\cos(\omega t)\) has two components:

\(A\sin(\omega t)\): can be in phase or 180° delayed relative to \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\), depending on the sign of \(A\).
\(B\cos(\omega t)\): is always 90° delayed relative to \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\). This term exists only because of damping (\(c = 0 \Rightarrow B = 0\)).

title: Class 4 — Damped Forced Vibration & Dimensionless Form
text:
4.2 Physical Amplitude and Phase
The components \(A\) and \(B\) alone are not the physical amplitude and phase — they are only the two contributions of the response. The actual physical amplitude \(U\) and phase angle \(\phi\) come from combining them:
\[U = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}, \qquad \phi = \arctan\!\left(\frac{-B}{A}\right)\]
Substituting the expressions for \(A\) and \(B\):






ImportantAmplitude and Phase of Damped Forced Response



\[\boxed{U = \frac{F_0}{\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}}\]
\[\boxed{\phi = \arctan\!\left(\frac{c\omega}{k - m\omega^2}\right)}\]
Unlike the undamped case, \(U\) is always finite — the damping term \((c\omega)^2\) prevents the denominator from ever reaching zero.

title: Class 4 — Damped Forced Vibration & Dimensionless Form
text:
4.3 Key Physical Conclusions

The Damping Term Eliminates the Singularity
At \(\omega = \omega_n\), we have \(k - m\omega_n^2 = 0\), so the denominator of \(U\) becomes:
\[(k - m\omega_n^2)^2 + (c\omega_n)^2 = 0 + (c\omega_n)^2 = (c\omega_n)^2\]
The term \((c\omega_n)^2\) eliminates the singularity that occurred in the undamped case. Also at \(\omega = \omega_n\):
\[A = \frac{F_0(k - m\omega_n^2)}{(c\omega_n)^2} = \frac{F_0 \cdot 0}{(c\omega_n)^2} = 0\]


At Resonance: Response Comes Only from B
Since \(A = 0\) at \(\omega = \omega_n\), the response is entirely governed by the cosine term:
\[u_p(t) = B\cos(\omega_n t), \qquad B = \frac{-F_0 c\omega_n}{(c\omega_n)^2} = -\frac{F_0}{c\omega_n}\]
Using the identity \(-\cos(\omega_n t) = \sin(\omega_n t - 90°)\):
\[\boxed{u_p(t) = \frac{F_0}{c\omega_n}\sin(\omega_n t - 90°)}\]






NoteTwo Important Conclusions at \(\omega = \omega_n\)




The amplitude is bounded: \(U = F_0/(c\omega_n)\). More damping → smaller resonant amplitude.
The displacement lags the force by exactly 90°. This is a key experimental signature of resonance and is used to identify \(\omega_n\) in vibration tests.

title: Class 4 — Damped Forced Vibration & Dimensionless Form
text:
4.4 Dimensionless Form
The physical form of the frequency response depends on five independent parameters: \(m\), \(k\), \(c\), \(F_0\), and \(\omega\). This means that every time we change the system — a different mass, a stiffer spring, a stronger force — we would need to recompute everything from scratch. There is no universal picture.
The dimensionless form solves this by collapsing those five parameters into just two dimensionless numbers: the frequency ratio \(r = \omega/\omega_n\) and the damping ratio \(\zeta = c/c_c\). The result is that:

A single plot of \(U/u_{st}\) vs \(r\) describes every possible 1-DOF system with the same \(\zeta\), regardless of the specific values of \(m\), \(k\), or \(F_0\).
We can immediately read off physical behaviour — stiffness-controlled (\(r \ll 1\)), mass-controlled (\(r \gg 1\)), or resonance-dominated (\(r \approx 1\)) — without solving anything.
The damping ratio \(\zeta\) becomes the single most important parameter: it controls the peak amplitude, the phase transition, and whether resonance is dangerous or benign.

This is why structural dynamics uses dimensionless form as the standard: one set of curves covers the entire design space.
To better analyse our systems in the future, we define a set of dimensionless parameters:






NoteDimensionless Parameters






Symbol
Name
Definition




\(\omega_n\)
Natural / resonance frequency
\(\sqrt{k/m}\)


\(r\)
Frequency ratio
\(\omega/\omega_n\)


\(c_c\)
Critical damping
\(2m\omega_n\)


\(\zeta\)
Damping ratio
\(c/c_c = c/(2m\omega_n)\)


\(u_{st}\)
Static displacement
\(F_0/k\)






Rewriting the Equation of Motion
Starting from \(m\ddot{u} + c\dot{u} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)\):
Step A — divide by \(m\):
\[\ddot{u} + \frac{c}{m}\dot{u} + \frac{k}{m}u = \frac{F_0}{m}\sin(\omega t)\]
Step B — substitute \(k/m = \omega_n^2\) and \(c/m = 2\zeta\omega_n\):






ImportantDimensionless Equation of Motion



\[\boxed{\ddot{u} + 2\zeta\omega_n\dot{u} + \omega_n^2 u = \frac{F_0}{m}\sin(\omega t)}\]
The equation is now described only by \(\omega_n\) and \(\zeta\).




Dimensionless Frequency Response
Applying the dimensionless parameters to \(U\) and \(\phi\):






ImportantDimensionless Frequency Response



\[\boxed{\frac{U}{u_{st}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2 + (2\zeta r)^2}}}\]
\[\boxed{\phi = \arctan\!\left(\frac{2\zeta r}{1-r^2}\right)}\]
These two curves fully characterise the 1-DOF forced response, independent of the specific values of \(m\), \(k\), or \(F_0\).

title: Class 4 — Damped Forced Vibration & Dimensionless Form
Class 6 — Transmissibility
text:
Imagine a mass \(m\) sitting on a spring \(k\) and a damper \(c\), driven by a harmonic force \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\). We already know from Class 4 how the mass moves. Now we ask the next engineering question:

What forces \(F_k\) and \(F_c\) are transmitted to the ground?

The spring and damper are the only mechanical links between mass and ground — all force reaching the support must pass through them. This is the problem of transmissibility.
General definition of transmissibility \(T\):
\[T = \frac{\text{transmitted output}}{\text{input excitation}}\]
Two physically distinct cases arise:
Case 1 — Force transmissibility: A machine vibrates and transmits force to the ground.
\[T_F = \frac{F_{t,0}}{F_0} = \frac{\text{output force amplitude}}{\text{input force amplitude}}\]
Case 2 — Motion transmissibility: The base/ground oscillates and transmits its movement to the mass.
\[T_R = \frac{x}{y} = \frac{\text{oscillation of the mass}}{\text{oscillation of the base}}\]

title: Class 6 — Transmissibility
text:
From Class 4, the steady-state response of a damped 1-DOF system under harmonic force \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\) is:
\[u(t) = U\sin(\omega t - \phi), \qquad \frac{U}{u_{st}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}\]
where \(r = \omega/\omega_n\) and \(\zeta = c/(2m\omega_n)\). We know the motion of the mass. This class asks the next engineering question: how much of the excitation passes through the isolators to the ground, or vice versa?

title: Class 6 — Transmissibility
text:
2 6.1 Transmissibility — General Concept
Transmissibility \(T\) is a dimensionless ratio comparing an output amplitude to the input that caused it:
\[T = \frac{\text{output amplitude}}{\text{input excitation amplitude}}\]
Two physically distinct configurations arise:






NoteTwo Transmissibility Scenarios












Force transmissibility \(T_F\)
Motion transmissibility \(T_x,\,T_u\)




Physical picture
Vibrating machine on mounts
Ground or vehicle base oscillates


Input
Force amplitude \(F_0\)
Base displacement amplitude \(Y\)


Output
Reaction force at support \(F_{t,0}\)
Mass motion: absolute \(X\) or relative \(U\)


Definition
\(T_F = F_{t,0}/F_0\)
\(T_x = X/Y\) or \(T_u = U/Y\)





Both scenarios lead to the same governing formula — a key result of this class.

title: Class 6 — Transmissibility
text:
6.2 Force Transmissibility

Physical Setup
A machine (mass \(m\)) sits on a spring–damper isolation mount and is driven by a harmonic force \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\). The spring and damper are the only mechanical connections to the ground — all force reaching the support must pass through them.





Left: machine on spring–damper mount driven by \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\). Right: the spring and damper are the only force paths to ground, transmitting \(F_k = ku\) and \(F_c = c\dot{u}\).


Transmitted Force Amplitude
The total instantaneous force at the support is the sum of the spring and damper reactions:
\[F_t(t) = k\,u(t) + c\,\dot{u}(t)\]
With the steady-state solution \(u(t) = U\sin(\omega t - \phi)\) and \(\dot{u}(t) = U\omega\cos(\omega t - \phi)\):
\[k\,u(t) = kU\sin(\omega t - \phi) \qquad \text{(elastic — in phase with }u\text{)}\]
\[c\,\dot{u}(t) = c\omega U\cos(\omega t - \phi) \qquad \text{(damping — 90° ahead of }u\text{)}\]
Since these two components are 90° out of phase, their amplitudes combine quadratically:
\[F_{t,0} = \sqrt{(kU)^2 + (c\omega U)^2} = U\sqrt{k^2 + (c\omega)^2}\]


Deriving the Transmissibility Formula
Substituting \(U = F_0/\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}\):
\[T_F = \frac{F_{t,0}}{F_0} = \frac{U\sqrt{k^2+(c\omega)^2}}{F_0} = \frac{\sqrt{k^2+(c\omega)^2}}{\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}\]
Dividing numerator and denominator by \(k\), and using \(r = \omega/\omega_n\), \(\zeta = c/(2m\omega_n)\):






ImportantForce Transmissibility



\[\boxed{T_F = \frac{\sqrt{1+(2\zeta r)^2}}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}}\]
This dimensionless function depends only on \(r\) (the frequency ratio) and \(\zeta\) (the damping ratio). It is plotted below and reveals three distinct operating regimes.

title: Class 6 — Transmissibility
text:
6.3 Interpreting the Transmissibility Curve

The Three Regimes





   Amplification T > 1 Isolation T < 1    r T   1   √2   0  1  2  3       Peak (r ≈ 1)   T = 1 for all ζ      


Transmissibility \(T_F\) versus frequency ratio \(r\). All curves (regardless of \(\zeta\)) pass through \(T = 1\) exactly at \(r = \sqrt{2}\), dividing the plot into an amplification zone and an isolation zone.




Regime-by-Regime Analysis
Low frequencies (\(r \ll 1\)) — No isolation
\[T \approx 1\]
The excitation is “slow” relative to the system. The mount deforms quasi-statically and transmits nearly all the force. No vibration isolation occurs.
Near resonance (\(r \approx 1\)) — Amplification
\[T > 1 \quad \text{(much greater than 1 for small }\zeta\text{)}\]
This is the worst operating region. The system magnifies the input — more force reaches the ground than was applied. Damping is essential here: increasing \(\zeta\) dramatically reduces the resonant peak.
High frequencies (\(r > \sqrt{2}\)) — Isolation
\[T < 1 \quad \text{(approaches 0 as }r \to \infty\text{)}\]
Real isolation begins. The isolator attenuates the transmitted force. To achieve isolation, the system must be designed so that \(\omega/\omega_n > \sqrt{2}\), i.e., \(\omega_n < \omega/\sqrt{2}\).






WarningThe Isolation Threshold and the Damping Dilemma



All transmissibility curves — regardless of \(\zeta\) — cross \(T = 1\) at exactly \(r = \sqrt{2}\). This is not a coincidence: setting \(T_F = 1\) and solving for \(r\) yields \(r = \sqrt{2}\) for any \(\zeta\).
Key trade-off: Damping helps near resonance (\(\zeta \uparrow \Rightarrow T_\text{max} \downarrow\)), but hurts in the isolation zone (\(r > \sqrt{2}\)): higher \(\zeta\) raises \(T\) above its undamped value. This is because at high frequencies the damper force \(c\dot{u} \sim c\omega U\) grows with frequency and increasingly dominates the ground reaction.
The ideal isolator has low stiffness (low \(\omega_n\), large \(r\)) and low damping — but must survive the startup transient through resonance.




Static Deflection Trade-off
To lower \(\omega_n\) (push the isolation zone to lower frequencies), we need softer springs: \(k \downarrow \Rightarrow \omega_n = \sqrt{k/m} \downarrow\). However, a softer spring causes larger static deflection under the weight of the machine:
\[\Delta_{st} = \frac{mg}{k}\]





A system with low \(k\) isolates better at high frequencies but suffers from a large static displacement \(\Delta_{st}\).
A system with lower \(k\) isolates better at high frequencies but sags more under its own weight. This is a fundamental engineering constraint — softer isolators require more travel clearance (e.g., air springs in precision instruments, soft suspension in vehicles).


Does Damping Always Help?
Now we come to an important question: does damping always help?
Answer:

Close to resonance (\(r \approx 1\)) it definitely helps: \(\zeta \uparrow \Rightarrow T_\text{max} \downarrow\).
But at high frequencies (\(r \gg 1\)) it can make things much worse. The total transmitted force is:

\[F_t(t) = k\,u(t) + c\,\dot{u}(t)\]
and since \(\dot{u} \sim \omega U\), the damping force grows with frequency. The higher the frequency, the higher the damping contribution to the transmitted force. Adding more damping at high \(r\) increases \(T_F\) rather than reducing it.
This is the fundamental trade-off of passive vibration isolation: the same damping that saves you at resonance hurts you in the isolation zone.

title: Class 6 — Transmissibility
text:
6.4 Motion Transmissibility — Base Excitation

Physical Setup
In many applications the ground itself vibrates: an earthquake shakes a building’s foundation, or road irregularities excite a vehicle. The problem is inverted — the input is a prescribed base motion \(y(t) = Y\sin(\omega t)\), and we ask how much motion reaches the mass.





Base excitation: the platform oscillates as \(y(t) = Y\sin(\omega t)\), driving the mass through the spring–damper mount. \(x(t)\) is the absolute displacement of the mass; \(u = x - y\) is the relative displacement.


Equation of Motion
The spring and damper forces depend on the relative deformation between mass and base:
\[F_k = k(x - y) = ku, \qquad F_c = c(\dot{x} - \dot{y}) = c\dot{u}\]
Applying Newton’s second law to the mass:
\[m\ddot{x} + c(\dot{x}-\dot{y}) + k(x-y) = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = c\dot{y} + ky\]


Relative Displacement \(u = x - y\)
Substituting \(x = u + y\) and \(\ddot{x} = \ddot{u} + \ddot{y}\):
\[m(\ddot{u}+\ddot{y}) + c\dot{u} + ku = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad m\ddot{u} + c\dot{u} + ku = -m\ddot{y}\]
With \(y(t) = Ye^{i\omega t}\), we have \(\ddot{y} = -\omega^2 Ye^{i\omega t}\), so the right-hand side \(-m\ddot{y} = m\omega^2 Ye^{i\omega t}\) acts like a harmonic inertial force of amplitude \(m\omega^2 Y\). Using complex notation:
\[\bigl(k - m\omega^2 + ic\omega\bigr)U = m\omega^2 Y \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{U}{Y} = \frac{m\omega^2}{k-m\omega^2+ic\omega}\]
Taking the modulus:






ImportantRelative Displacement Transmissibility



\[\boxed{\frac{U}{Y} = \frac{r^2}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}}\]
This gives the amplitude of the mount’s deformation relative to the base oscillation amplitude \(Y\). It equals zero at \(r = 0\) (rigid-body motion) and approaches 1 as \(r \to \infty\).

title: Class 6 — Transmissibility
text:
6.5 Absolute Displacement Transmissibility
For the absolute displacement \(x(t)\), we return to the equation \(m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = c\dot{y} + ky\).
With \(y(t) = Ye^{i\omega t}\) and \(x(t) = Xe^{i\omega t}\):
\[(-m\omega^2 + ic\omega + k)\,X = (k + ic\omega)\,Y \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{X}{Y} = \frac{k + ic\omega}{k - m\omega^2 + ic\omega}\]
Taking the modulus:
\[T_x = \frac{X}{Y} = \frac{\sqrt{k^2+(c\omega)^2}}{\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}\]






ImportantAbsolute Motion Transmissibility = Force Transmissibility



\[\boxed{T_x = \frac{X}{Y} = \frac{\sqrt{1+(2\zeta r)^2}}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}} = T_F}\]
The formula is identical to the force transmissibility. This elegant result means the same plot and the same design rules apply to both problems: a machine on isolators and a structure on a shaking foundation.

text:

In the high-frequency regime, the mass is essentially stationary in space while the base oscillates beneath it — the ideal seismic isolation condition. The mount must accommodate the full relative displacement \(u \approx y\).

Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
In Class 7, we studied the free 2DOF system. Now we add the harmonic force. A 2DOF system has two independent coordinates, so it will have two natural frequencies and two vibration modes.
In a 1DOF system we saw:
\[m\ddot{u} + ku = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad m\ddot{u} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)\]
The same idea applies to our 2DOF system:
\[\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{F}_0\sin(\omega t)}\]
where \(\mathbf{F}_0 = [F_{01},\, F_{02}]^T\) is the excitation force vector. This means the force can be applied to mass 1, mass 2, or both masses.

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
In Class 7, we studied the free 2DOF system. Now we add the harmonic force. A 2DOF system has two independent coordinates, so it will have two natural frequencies and two vibration modes.
In a 1DOF system we saw:
\[m\ddot{u} + ku = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad m\ddot{u} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)\]
The same idea applies to our 2DOF system:
\[\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{F}_0\sin(\omega t)}\]
where \(\mathbf{F}_0 = [F_{01},\, F_{02}]^T\) is the excitation force vector. This means the force can be applied to mass 1, mass 2, or both masses.

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.2 The System for This Class
We use the same 2DOF system as in Class 7, but now apply a harmonic force to mass 1 only:





The equations of motion are:
\[m_1\ddot{u}_1 + (k_1+k_2)u_1 - k_2 u_2 = F_0\sin(\omega t)\] \[m_2\ddot{u}_2 - k_2 u_1 + k_2 u_2 = 0\]
In matrix form:
\[\begin{bmatrix} m_1 & 0 \\ 0 & m_2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \ddot{u}_1 \\ \ddot{u}_2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} k_1+k_2 & -k_2 \\ -k_2 & k_2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} F_0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\sin(\omega t)\]

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.3 Harmonic Steady-State Response
For a linear system excited harmonically, the steady-state response occurs at the same frequency as the excitation. We assume:
\[u_1(t) = U_1\sin(\omega t), \qquad u_2(t) = U_2\sin(\omega t)\]
or in matrix form:
\[\boxed{\mathbf{u}(t) = \mathbf{U}\sin(\omega t)}, \qquad \mathbf{U} = \begin{bmatrix} U_1 \\ U_2 \end{bmatrix}\]
The acceleration is \(\ddot{\mathbf{u}} = -\omega^2\mathbf{U}\sin(\omega t)\). Substituting into the equation of motion and cancelling \(\sin(\omega t)\):
\[\boxed{(\mathbf{K} - \omega^2\mathbf{M})\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{F}_0}\]

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.4 The Dynamic Stiffness Matrix
Define the dynamic stiffness matrix:
\[\boxed{\mathbf{D}(\omega) = \mathbf{K} - \omega^2\mathbf{M}}\]
Then:
\[\mathbf{D}(\omega)\,\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{F}_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{D}^{-1}(\omega)\,\mathbf{F}_0}\]
provided \(\mathbf{D}(\omega)\) is invertible. For our system:
\[\mathbf{D}(\omega) = \begin{bmatrix} k_1+k_2-m_1\omega^2 & -k_2 \\ -k_2 & k_2-m_2\omega^2 \end{bmatrix}\]
The two algebraic equations for the response amplitudes are:
\[(k_1+k_2-m_1\omega^2)U_1 - k_2 U_2 = F_0 \tag{1}\] \[-k_2 U_1 + (k_2-m_2\omega^2)U_2 = 0 \tag{2}\]

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.5 Solving for the Response Amplitudes
From equation (2):
\[(k_2 - m_2\omega^2)U_2 = k_2 U_1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad U_2 = \frac{k_2}{k_2-m_2\omega^2}\,U_1\]
Substituting into equation (1) and solving for \(U_1\):
\[\left[(k_1+k_2-m_1\omega^2) - \frac{k_2^2}{k_2-m_2\omega^2}\right]U_1 = F_0\]
\[\frac{(k_1+k_2-m_1\omega^2)(k_2-m_2\omega^2) - k_2^2}{k_2-m_2\omega^2}\,U_1 = F_0\]
Therefore:






ImportantMost Important Equation of This Class



\[\boxed{\frac{U_1}{F_0} = \frac{k_2 - m_2\omega^2}{(k_1+k_2-m_1\omega^2)(k_2-m_2\omega^2) - k_2^2}}\]
The numerator and denominator independently control the two key phenomena: resonance and anti-resonance.

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.6 Resonance and Anti-Resonance

Resonance
Resonance occurs when the denominator equals zero:
\[(k_1+k_2-m_1\omega^2)(k_2-m_2\omega^2) - k_2^2 = 0\]
This is exactly the determinant condition from Class 7 — \(\det(\mathbf{D}(\omega)) = 0\) — so resonance occurs at the two natural frequencies \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\).


Anti-Resonance
Anti-resonance occurs when the numerator equals zero:
\[k_2 - m_2\omega^2 = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k_2}{m_2}}}\]
At this frequency, \(U_1 = 0\): the force is applied to mass 1, but mass 1 does not move. The second mass vibrates and absorbs all the energy — this is the principle of the dynamic vibration absorber.

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.7 The Dynamic Vibration Absorber
The system can be interpreted as a primary system plus an absorber:





The absorber has its own natural frequency:
\[\omega_a = \sqrt{\frac{k_2}{m_2}}\]
The anti-resonance condition is \(\omega = \omega_a\). To suppress vibration of \(m_1\) at the excitation frequency, we tune the absorber so that its natural frequency matches the forcing frequency:
\[\sqrt{\frac{k_1}{m_1}} = \sqrt{\frac{k_2}{m_2}} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \boxed{k_2 = m_2\,\omega^2}\]
The parameters \(k_2\) and \(m_2\) must be selected to satisfy this tuning condition.

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.8 Physical Interpretation at Anti-Resonance
At anti-resonance (\(U_1 = 0\)), the first equation of motion becomes:
\[(k_1+k_2-m_1\omega^2)\cdot 0 - k_2 U_2 = F_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{U_2 = -\frac{F_0}{k_2}}\]
The absorber mass moves with amplitude \(F_0/k_2\) in the opposite direction to the applied force. The spring force \(-k_2 U_2 = F_0\) exactly cancels the applied force on mass 1 — that is why \(m_1\) does not move.
This also shows a practical constraint: the absorber must have enough stroke to accommodate this displacement.

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.9 Dimensionless Form
It is useful to express the response in dimensionless parameters.
Define the primary natural frequency: \(\omega_1^{(0)} = \sqrt{k_1/m_1}\)
Define the frequency ratio: \(r = \omega/\omega_1^{(0)}\)
Define the tuning ratio: \(f = \omega_a/\omega_1^{(0)}\), where \(\omega_a = \sqrt{k_2/m_2}\)
Define the mass ratio: \(\mu = m_2/m_1\)
Define the static displacement: \(u_{st} = F_0/k_1\)
The dimensionless primary response becomes:
\[\boxed{\frac{U_1}{u_{st}} = \frac{f^2-r^2}{(1+\mu f^2-r^2)(f^2-r^2) - \mu f^4}}\]
When \(r = f\) (tuning condition), the numerator is zero and \(U_1 = 0\) — this is anti-resonance.

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.10 Design Trade-Off: Absorber Mass
The mass ratio \(\mu = m_2/m_1\) controls the trade-off:

A larger absorber mass spreads the two resonance peaks further apart, making the anti-resonance zone wider and more robust.
A heavier absorber adds weight — often undesirable in practice.

The absorber suppresses vibration exactly at one frequency (\(r = f\)) but introduces two new resonances nearby. Real absorbers often include damping to reduce these peaks at the cost of a non-zero response at the tuning frequency.







Without damping
With damping




\(U_1 = 0\) exactly at \(\omega = \omega_a\)
\(U_1 \neq 0\) at \(\omega = \omega_a\)


Two sharp resonance peaks
Two reduced resonance peaks


Sensitive to detuning
More robust to frequency variation

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.11 Numerical Design Example
Given: Machine modeled as a primary SDOF system with \(m_1 = 10\,\text{kg}\), \(k_1 = 1000\,\text{N/m}\), excited at its natural frequency.
Step 1 — Primary natural frequency:
\[\omega_1^{(0)} = \sqrt{\frac{k_1}{m_1}} = \sqrt{\frac{1000}{10}} = 10\,\text{rad/s}\]
Step 2 — Choose mass ratio \(\mu = 0.1\):
\[m_2 = \mu m_1 = 0.1 \times 10 = 1\,\text{kg}\]
Step 3 — Tune absorber to \(\omega_a = \omega_1^{(0)} = 10\,\text{rad/s}\):
\[k_2 = m_2\,\omega_a^2 = 1 \times 10^2 = \boxed{100\,\text{N/m}}\]
Result: \(m_2 = 1\,\text{kg}\), \(k_2 = 100\,\text{N/m}\) — the absorber suppresses vibration of \(m_1\) at \(\omega = 10\,\text{rad/s}\).
Absorber displacement at the tuning frequency (for \(F_0 = 10\,\text{N}\)):
\[U_2 = -\frac{F_0}{k_2} = -\frac{10}{100} = -0.1\,\text{m}\]
The absorber must be designed to accommodate \(\pm 100\,\text{mm}\) of stroke.

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.12 Key Messages

Forced 2DOF equation: \(\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{F}_0\sin(\omega t)\)
Harmonic assumption gives: \((\mathbf{K} - \omega^2\mathbf{M})\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{F}_0\)
Dynamic stiffness matrix: \(\mathbf{D}(\omega) = \mathbf{K} - \omega^2\mathbf{M}\)
Resonance when \(\det(\mathbf{D}(\omega)) = 0\) — at the natural frequencies \(\omega_1\), \(\omega_2\).
Anti-resonance when numerator = 0: \(k_2 - m_2\omega^2 = 0 \Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{k_2/m_2}\)
Primary response: \(U_1/F_0 = (k_2-m_2\omega^2)\,/\,\det(\mathbf{D})\)
Tuning condition: \(k_2 = m_2\omega^2\) — tune absorber to forcing frequency.
At the tuning frequency: \(U_1 = 0\) and \(U_2 = -F_0/k_2\).
The absorber creates a zero-response notch but introduces two new resonance peaks.
Practical absorbers include damping to reduce peak severity at the cost of perfect cancellation.

title: Class 8 — Forced Vibration of 2DOF Systems
text:
8.13 What Comes Next
In this class, we used a 2DOF system as a dynamic vibration absorber. We found that, without damping, the absorber gives perfect vibration cancellation at one frequency but creates two new resonances.
The natural next step is to include damping in 2DOF systems:
\[\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{C}\dot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{F}_0\sin(\omega t)\]
This will allow us to study more realistic absorbers and understand the optimal damping ratio that minimises the response over the widest frequency range.

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
In our last class, we analyzed the transfer of forces to the base of a 1DOF system. Now, imagine that instead of a base or ground, we have another mass. Let us see how this works by studying a unit mass connected to another mass.
The system we will analyze is:





Displacements \(u_1(t)\) and \(u_2(t)\) are measured positive to the right from the equilibrium position of each mass.






NoteCoordinates



We need two independent coordinates \(u_1(t)\) and \(u_2(t)\) — one per mass. Each coordinate is measured from the static equilibrium position of that mass. This is the key difference from the SDOF case: one equation of motion is no longer enough.


The spring \(k_2\) couples the two masses. The motion of \(m_1\) affects \(m_2\), and vice versa. If \(k_2 = 0\), the two masses would be independent 1DOF oscillators.

In our last class, we analyzed the transfer of forces to the base of a 1DOF system. Now, imagine that instead of a base or ground, we have another mass. Let us see how this works by studying a unit mass connected to another mass.
The system we will analyze is:





Displacements \(u_1(t)\) and \(u_2(t)\) are measured positive to the right from the equilibrium position of each mass.






NoteCoordinates



We need two independent coordinates \(u_1(t)\) and \(u_2(t)\) — one per mass. Each coordinate is measured from the static equilibrium position of that mass. This is the key difference from the SDOF case: one equation of motion is no longer enough.


The spring \(k_2\) couples the two masses. The motion of \(m_1\) affects \(m_2\), and vice versa. If \(k_2 = 0\), the two masses would be independent 1DOF oscillators.

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
7.2 Free-Body Diagrams
We take positive displacement to the right.






Mass 1
Spring \(k_1\) is attached to the wall. Its deformation is \(u_1\), so the force on \(m_1\) is \(-k_1 u_1\).
Spring \(k_2\) connects both masses. Its deformation is \(u_2 - u_1\), so the force on \(m_1\) is \(k_2(u_2 - u_1)\).
Applying Newton’s second law:
\[m_1\ddot{u}_1 = -k_1 u_1 + k_2(u_2 - u_1)\]
Rearranging:
\[\boxed{m_1\ddot{u}_1 + (k_1+k_2)u_1 - k_2 u_2 = 0}\]


Mass 2
Only spring \(k_2\) acts on \(m_2\). The restoring force is \(-k_2(u_2 - u_1)\):
\[m_2\ddot{u}_2 = -k_2(u_2 - u_1)\]
Rearranging:
\[\boxed{m_2\ddot{u}_2 - k_2 u_1 + k_2 u_2 = 0}\]

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
7.3 Coupled Equations of Motion
The two equations are:
\[m_1\ddot{u}_1 + (k_1+k_2)u_1 - k_2 u_2 = 0\] \[m_2\ddot{u}_2 - k_2 u_1 + k_2 u_2 = 0\]
Notice the coupling terms: \(-k_2 u_2\) in the first equation and \(-k_2 u_1\) in the second. Both come from the spring \(k_2\) connecting the two masses. If \(k_2 = 0\), the equations decouple into two independent SDOF problems.

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
7.4 Matrix Form
The equations can be written compactly as:
\[\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}\]
where:
\[\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} m_1 & 0 \\ 0 & m_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} k_1+k_2 & -k_2 \\ -k_2 & k_2 \end{bmatrix}\]
Therefore:
\[\boxed{\begin{bmatrix} m_1 & 0 \\ 0 & m_2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \ddot{u}_1 \\ \ddot{u}_2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} k_1+k_2 & -k_2 \\ -k_2 & k_2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}\]
The diagonal terms of \(\mathbf{K}\) represent stiffnesses directly connected to each coordinate. The off-diagonal terms \(-k_2\) represent the elastic coupling between coordinates.

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
7.5 Assuming Harmonic Motion
In a natural mode, both coordinates vibrate at the same frequency with different amplitudes. We assume:
\[u_1(t) = \phi_1\sin(\omega t), \qquad u_2(t) = \phi_2\sin(\omega t)\]
or, in matrix form:
\[\boxed{\mathbf{u}(t) = \boldsymbol{\phi}\sin(\omega t)}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\phi} = \begin{bmatrix} \phi_1 \\ \phi_2 \end{bmatrix}\]
The vector \(\boldsymbol{\phi}\) is called the mode shape. It describes the relative amplitudes of the two coordinates during a natural vibration.
The acceleration is:
\[\ddot{\mathbf{u}}(t) = -\omega^2\boldsymbol{\phi}\sin(\omega t)\]

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
7.6 The Eigenvalue Problem
Substituting into \(\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}\):
\[\left[-\omega^2\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\phi} + \mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{\phi}\right]\sin(\omega t) = \mathbf{0}\]
Since this must hold for all \(t\), we can divide through by \(\sin(\omega t)\):






ImportantVery Important Equation



\[\boxed{(\mathbf{K} - \omega^2\mathbf{M})\boldsymbol{\phi} = \mathbf{0}}\]
This is the eigenvalue problem for free vibration. All natural frequencies and mode shapes of the system come from this single equation.

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
7.7 Natural Frequencies
The eigenvalue problem has the trivial solution \(\boldsymbol{\phi} = \mathbf{0}\) (no motion). For a non-trivial solution, the matrix \(\mathbf{K} - \omega^2\mathbf{M}\) must be singular:
\[\boxed{\det(\mathbf{K} - \omega^2\mathbf{M}) = 0}\]
This is the frequency equation (characteristic equation).
For our system:
\[\mathbf{K} - \omega^2\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} k_1+k_2-m_1\omega^2 & -k_2 \\ -k_2 & k_2-m_2\omega^2 \end{bmatrix}\]
Setting the determinant to zero:
\[(k_1+k_2-m_1\omega^2)(k_2-m_2\omega^2) - k_2^2 = 0\]
Expanding:
\[(k_1+k_2)k_2 - (k_1+k_2)m_2\omega^2 - m_1 k_2\omega^2 + m_1 m_2\omega^4 - k_2^2 = 0\]
The constant terms simplify:
\[(k_1+k_2)k_2 - k_2^2 = k_1 k_2 + k_2^2 - k_2^2 = k_1 k_2\]
So:
\[\boxed{m_1 m_2\,\omega^4 - \bigl[(k_1+k_2)m_2 + m_1 k_2\bigr]\omega^2 + k_1 k_2 = 0}\]
This is a quadratic in \(\omega^2\). Let \(\lambda = \omega^2\):
\[m_1 m_2\,\lambda^2 - \bigl[(k_1+k_2)m_2 + m_1 k_2\bigr]\lambda + k_1 k_2 = 0\]
Solving gives two values \(\lambda_1 = \omega_1^2 < \lambda_2 = \omega_2^2\), hence two natural frequencies \(\omega_1 < \omega_2\).

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
section: 7.8 Simplified Case: Equal Masses and Equal Springs
text:
7.8 Simplified Case: Equal Masses and Equal Springs
Let \(m_1 = m_2 = m\) and \(k_1 = k_2 = k\). Then:
\[\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} m & 0 \\ 0 & m \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} 2k & -k \\ -k & k \end{bmatrix}\]
The frequency equation becomes:
\[(2k - m\omega^2)(k - m\omega^2) - k^2 = 0\]
\[m^2\omega^4 - 3km\,\omega^2 + k^2 = 0\]
Using the quadratic formula with \(\lambda = \omega^2\):
\[\lambda = \frac{k}{m}\,\frac{3 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}\]
Therefore:
\[\boxed{\omega_1 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}\cdot\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}} \approx 0.618\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}}\]
\[\boxed{\omega_2 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}\cdot\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}} \approx 1.618\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}}\]
The golden ratio \(\varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2 \approx 1.618\) appears naturally in this symmetric system.

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
7.9 Mode Shapes
Once a natural frequency \(\omega_i\) is known, the mode shape follows from:
\[(\mathbf{K} - \omega_i^2\mathbf{M})\boldsymbol{\phi}_i = \mathbf{0}\]
For the simplified case, the first row gives:
\[(2k - m\omega_i^2)\phi_{1i} - k\phi_{2i} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\phi_{2i}}{\phi_{1i}} = 2 - \frac{m\omega_i^2}{k}\]
Choosing \(\phi_{1i} = 1\) (the absolute scale is arbitrary):

First Mode (\(\omega_1\))
\[\frac{m\omega_1^2}{k} = \frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\phi_{21}}{\phi_{11}} = \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 1.618\]
\[\boxed{\boldsymbol{\phi}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1.618 \end{bmatrix}}\]
Both masses move in the same direction; mass 2 moves more than mass 1. This is the lower-frequency (softer) mode.


Second Mode (\(\omega_2\))
\[\frac{m\omega_2^2}{k} = \frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\phi_{22}}{\phi_{12}} = \frac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2} \approx -0.618\]
\[\boxed{\boldsymbol{\phi}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -0.618 \end{bmatrix}}\]
The masses move in opposite directions. This is the higher-frequency (stiffer) mode, because the connecting spring is strongly compressed.

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
7.10 Why Either Equation Works
After substituting a natural frequency \(\omega_i\) into \((\mathbf{K} - \omega_i^2\mathbf{M})\boldsymbol{\phi}_i = \mathbf{0}\), the two scalar equations become linearly dependent — this is guaranteed because \(\det(\mathbf{K} - \omega_i^2\mathbf{M}) = 0\). Therefore, either row gives the same mode shape ratio.
The absolute magnitude of a mode shape is arbitrary. Only the ratio \(\phi_{2i}/\phi_{1i}\) has physical meaning.

text:
7.11 Physical Interpretation

In Mode 1, the connecting spring is gently stretched (both masses go the same way). In Mode 2, the connecting spring is strongly deformed (masses oppose each other), explaining the higher frequency.

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
7.12 Key Messages

A 2DOF system needs two independent coordinates \(u_1(t)\), \(u_2(t)\).
The equations of motion are coupled through the connecting spring \(k_2\).
Matrix form: \(\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}\).
Assuming harmonic motion gives the eigenvalue problem: \((\mathbf{K} - \omega^2\mathbf{M})\boldsymbol{\phi} = \mathbf{0}\).
Natural frequencies come from \(\det(\mathbf{K} - \omega^2\mathbf{M}) = 0\), which is a quadratic in \(\omega^2\).
A 2DOF system has two natural frequencies \(\omega_1 < \omega_2\) and two mode shapes \(\boldsymbol{\phi}_1\), \(\boldsymbol{\phi}_2\).
Mode shapes give only relative amplitudes — their absolute scale is arbitrary.

title: Class 7 — Introduction to 2DOF Systems
text:
7.13 What Comes Next
In this class we studied free, undamped vibration: \(\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}\).
The next step is forced vibration:
\[\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{F}_0\sin(\omega t)\]
This will allow us to understand vibration absorbers, tuned mass dampers, multiple resonances, and the phenomenon of anti-resonance.

title: Class 3 — Forced Vibration of Undamped Systems
text:
3.3 Finding the Forced Harmonic Response
Starting from \(m\ddot{u} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)\), substitute the trial \(u_p(t) = U\sin(\omega t)\):
\[\dot{u}_p(t) = U\omega\cos(\omega t), \qquad \ddot{u}_p(t) = -U\omega^2\sin(\omega t)\]
Substituting into the equation of motion:
\[m\bigl(-U\omega^2\bigr)\sin(\omega t) + kU\sin(\omega t) = F_0\sin(\omega t)\]
Dividing through by \(\sin(\omega t)\):
\[-mU\omega^2 + kU = F_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad U(k - m\omega^2) = F_0\]
\[\boxed{U = \frac{F_0}{k - m\omega^2}}\]
Dividing numerator and denominator by \(k\) and using \(k/m = \omega_n^2\):
\[\boxed{U = \frac{F_0/k}{1 - \left(\dfrac{\omega}{\omega_n}\right)^2}}\]
The quantity \(F_0/k\) is the static deflection — the displacement under a static force \(F_0\).

Case 1: \(\omega < \omega_n\)
\[\omega_n^2 - \omega^2 > 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad U > 0\]
The particular response is \(u_p(t) = U\sin(\omega t)\): force \(F(t)\) and response \(u_p(t)\) point in the same direction.
\[\longrightarrow F(t) \qquad \longrightarrow u_p(t)\]


Case 2: \(\omega > \omega_n\)
\[\omega_n^2 - \omega^2 < 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad U < 0\]
Writing \(U = -|U|\):
\[u_p(t) = -|U|\sin(\omega t) = |U|\sin(\omega t + \pi)\]
Force and response point in opposite directions — the mass moves against the force.
\[\longrightarrow F(t) \qquad \longleftarrow u_p(t)\]


Phase Shift at \(\omega = \omega_n\)
As \(\omega\) crosses \(\omega_n\), the denominator changes sign and the phase jumps discontinuously from 0° to 180°:
\[\text{Phase} = \begin{cases} 0° & \omega < \omega_n \\ 180° & \omega > \omega_n \end{cases}\]


Why Does This Shift Happen?
Substituting \(u_p\) back into the equation of motion:
\[m\ddot{u}_p + ku_p = U\,(k - m\omega^2)\sin(\omega t)\]
The bracket \(k - m\omega^2\) changes sign at \(\omega = \omega_n\):

For \(\omega < \omega_n\): the stiffness \(k\) dominates — the system is stiffness-controlled.
For \(\omega > \omega_n\): the inertia \(m\omega^2\) dominates — the system is mass-controlled, and the sign of \(U\) flips.

title: Class 4 — Damped Forced Vibration & Dimensionless Form
text:
Systems without damping are an idealization. Real structures dissipate energy through damping — viscous, dry friction, and other mechanisms.
In undamped systems, the free response \(u_h(t)\) never disappears:
\[u(t) = u_h(t) + u_p(t)\]
Damping introduces energy dissipation to our systems, and they become physically realistic: \(u_h(t)\) eventually decays, leaving only the steady-state particular response \(u_p(t)\).
Our forced damped system is governed by:
\[\boxed{m\ddot{u} + \underset{=}{c\dot{u}} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)}\]
Similarly to the undamped case, we try a particular solution:
\[u_p(t) = A\sin(\omega t) + B\cos(\omega t)\]






WarningWhy a cosine term?



In the undamped case, a pure sine \(u_p = U\sin(\omega t)\) was sufficient. With damping, the \(c\dot{u}\) term introduces a component proportional to \(\cos(\omega t)\), so we need two components. If \(c = 0\), we will find \(B = 0\) and recover the undamped result.




Computing derivatives of the trial solution:
\[\dot{u}_p(t) = A\omega\cos(\omega t) - B\omega\sin(\omega t)\] \[\ddot{u}_p(t) = -A\omega^2\sin(\omega t) - B\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\]
Substituting into the equation of motion term by term:

Inertia term: \(m\ddot{u}_p = -mA\omega^2\sin(\omega t) - mB\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\)
Damping term: \(c\dot{u}_p = \phantom{-}cA\omega\cos(\omega t) - cB\omega\sin(\omega t)\)
Elastic term: \(ku_p = \phantom{-m}kA\sin(\omega t) + kB\cos(\omega t)\)

Grouping by \(\sin(\omega t)\) and \(\cos(\omega t)\) and setting equal to \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\):
\[\underbrace{[A(k-m\omega^2) - cB\omega]}_{\alpha}\sin(\omega t) + \underbrace{[B(k-m\omega^2) + cA\omega]}_{\beta}\cos(\omega t) = F_0\sin(\omega t)\]
For this to hold at all times \(t\):
\[\alpha = F_0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \beta = 0\]
Defining \(D = k - m\omega^2\) for convenience:
\[\begin{cases} AD - cB\omega = F_0 \\ BD + cA\omega = 0 \end{cases}\]
Solving this \(2\times 2\) system:
\[\boxed{A = \frac{F_0 D}{D^2+(c\omega)^2} = \frac{F_0(k-m\omega^2)}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}\]
\[\boxed{B = -\frac{c\omega A}{D} = \frac{-F_0 c\omega}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}\]
Therefore:
\[u_p(t) = A\sin(\omega t) + B\cos(\omega t)\]



The two components play different roles:

\(A\sin(\omega t)\): can only be in phase (\(A > 0\)) or 180° delayed (\(A < 0\)) relative to \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\).
\(B\cos(\omega t)\): is always 90° delayed relative to \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\).

Note that \(B = -F_0 c\omega\big/[D^2 + (c\omega)^2]\): if \(c = 0\) then \(B = 0\) — the 90°-delayed component only exists because of damping \(c\).

title: Class 5 — Free Damped Systems
text:
Case 2 — Critically Damped System (\(\zeta = 1\))
When \(\zeta = 1\), the discriminant vanishes and \(s = -\omega_n\) is a repeated root:
\[s^2 + 2\omega_n s + \omega_n^2 = (s + \omega_n)^2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad S_1 = S_2 = -\omega_n\]
Since the equation is second order, we need two independent solutions. The first is:
\[u_1(t) = A\,e^{-\omega_n t}\]
The second independent solution comes from the theory of repeated roots (Taylor expansion):
\[u_2(t) = Bt\,e^{-\omega_n t}\]
The complete critically damped solution is:






ImportantCritically Damped Free Response



\[\boxed{u(t) = (A + Bt)\,e^{-\omega_n t}}\]
Critical damping returns the system to equilibrium as fast as possible without any oscillation.

title: Class 5 — Free Damped Systems
text:
Case 3 — Overdamped System (\(\zeta > 1\))
When \(\zeta > 1\), both roots are real and distinct:
\[s_1 = -\zeta\omega_n + \omega_n\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}, \qquad s_2 = -\zeta\omega_n - \omega_n\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\]
The general solution is:






ImportantOverdamped Free Response



\[\boxed{u(t) = A\,e^{s_1 t} + B\,e^{s_2 t}}\]
Since \(s_1 < 0\) and \(s_2 < 0\), both terms decay exponentially — the response is non-oscillatory and slower than critical damping.




Summary: The Three Damping Regimes
The discriminant \(\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\) controls the qualitative behaviour. \(\zeta\) controls the qualitative motion of the system.

title: Class 6 — Transmissibility
text:
Imagine a mass \(m\) sitting on a spring \(k\) and a damper \(c\), driven by a harmonic force \(F_0\sin(\omega t)\). We already know from Class 4 how the mass moves. Now we ask the next engineering question:

What forces \(F_k\) and \(F_c\) are transmitted to the ground?

The spring and damper are the only mechanical links between mass and ground — all force reaching the support must pass through them. This is the problem of transmissibility.
General definition of transmissibility \(T\):
\[T = \frac{\text{transmitted output}}{\text{input excitation}}\]
Two physically distinct cases arise:
Case 1 — Force transmissibility: A machine vibrates and transmits force to the ground.
\[T_F = \frac{F_{t,0}}{F_0} = \frac{\text{output force amplitude}}{\text{input force amplitude}}\]
Case 2 — Motion transmissibility: The base/ground oscillates and transmits its movement to the mass.
\[T_R = \frac{x}{y} = \frac{\text{oscillation of the mass}}{\text{oscillation of the base}}\]

title: Class 2 — Springs, Dampers & Equation of Motion
text:
What Comes Next
In this class we derived the equation of motion and studied the free, undamped response: the system oscillates indefinitely at \(\omega_n\) with no energy loss.
In reality, structures are driven by external forces. In Class 3 we add a harmonic excitation to the right-hand side:
\[m\ddot{u} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)\]
This will reveal the phenomenon of resonance — what happens when the excitation frequency \(\omega\) approaches the natural frequency \(\omega_n\).
